'''Daniel Harry Friedan''' (born October 3, 1948)<ref>Judith Adler Hennessee, ''Betty Friedan: her life'', Random House, 1999, p.50<!--"Daniel Friedan was born on October 3, 1948, at the Flower-Fifth Avenue Hospital."--></ref> is an American theoretical physicist and a professor at [[Rutgers University]]. He is one of three children of the feminist author and activist [[Betty Friedan]].<ref>[https://www.usatoday.com/news/nation/2006-02-04-friedan-obit_x.htm Feminist author, icon Betty Friedan dies at 85], ''[[USA Today]]'',  February 4, 2006. Accessed August 1, 2011</ref>

==Biography==
===Education and career===
Friedan earned his Ph.D. from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1980 and was named a [[MacArthur Fellow]] in 1987.<ref>[http://news.rutgers.edu/medrel/news-releases/2010/03/american-physical-so-20100310 American Physical Society Recognizes Rutgers Professors for Outstanding Research], [[Rutgers University]] newstelease, March 16, 2010. Accessed August 1, 2011</ref><ref>[https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/washingtonpost/access/73827371.html?dids=73827371:73827371&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Jun+16%2C+1987&author=Victoria+Dawson&pub=The+Washington+Post+(pre-1997+Fulltext)&desc=MacArthur+%60Genius+Awards'+To+32%3B+Honors+List+Includes+Washington+Writer&pqatl=google MacArthur `Genius Awards' To 32; Honors List Includes Washington Writer]{{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307083420/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/washingtonpost/doc/306938566.html?FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Jun%2016,%201987&author=Victoria%20Dawson&pub=The%20Washington%20Post%20(pre-1997%20Fulltext)&edition=&startpage=&desc=MacArthur%20%60Genius%20Awards%27%20To%2032;%20Honors%20List%20Includes%20Washington%20Writer |archive-date=7 March 2016}}, ''[[The Washington Post]]'', June 16, 1987</ref>

In 1979, he showed that the equations of motions of string theory, which are generalizations of the [[Einstein equations]] of [[general relativity]], emerge from the [[renormalization group]] equations for the two-dimensional field theory.<ref>D. Friedan, unpublished lectures given at the Mathematics and Physics Conference (Durham, England, July 1979), at the Nuffield Workshop on Quantum Gravity (Cambridge, England, August 13, 1979), and at the Nato Advanced Study Institute on Recent Developments in Gauge Theories (Cargese, France, August 1979), and unpublished manuscript, "Geometric Models for Critical Systems in 2 + ε Dimensions," subtitled "Expanded Version of a talk given at the Nuffield Workshop on Quantum Gravity, DAMTP, Cambridge University, August 13, 1979," commissioned by the directors of the 1979 Nuffield Workshop, and privately circulated to them at the conclusion of the workshop. See also {{arXiv|hep-ph/0204131}}.</ref>

Friedan has worked in [[string theory]] and [[condensed matter]] theory, specializing in (1&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)-dimensional systems. His current research focuses on applications to [[quantum computers]].

Friedan received the 2010 [[Lars Onsager Prize]] from the [[American Physical Society]] "for seminal work on the classification and characterization of two-dimensional unitary conformal field theories of critical states."<ref>[http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Friedan&first_nm=Daniel&year=2010 2010 Lars Onsager Prize Recipient], [[American Physical Society]]. Accessed August 1, 2011</ref> He currently teaches at [[Rutgers University]].

==Personal life==
Daniel is married to an Icelandic physics teacher, Ragnheiður Guðmundsdóttir. They have two daughters and one son together.
